analysis.one_liner: Automatically enrolls every child born after 2006 in a Medicare-style government health plan from birth to age 23.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2005 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a program called MediKids that automatically enrolls every child born after December 31, 2006 in government health coverage modeled on Medicare, running through age 23. Benefits would include doctor and hospital care plus prescription drugs, with reduced or no out-of-pocket costs for low-income families. Families would pay a modest premium through their tax return, capped at 5% of income, with very low-income families exempt. A family could instead use private insurance, Medicaid, or SCHIP, but MediKids would remain the backup whenever other coverage lapses.
analysis.who_benefits: All children born after 2006, who would be covered from birth without enrollment gaps. Low-income families gain the most: no cost-sharing below 150% of the poverty line, premiums waived below roughly $19,000 of income, and premium phaseouts above that. Families whose coverage changes with jobs, income, or marital status would always have a fallback plan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children born after 2006, especially low-income families

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after December 31, 2006 would be deemed enrolled in MediKids at birth, eliminating the outreach and eligibility gaps that leave children uninsured even under Medicaid and SCHIP.
Benefits would include Medicare core benefits, all mandatory Medicaid benefits for children, and prescription drug coverage no worse than the federal employee standard plan in 2005.

Children in families below 150% of poverty would pay no cost-sharing; those between 150% and 300% of poverty would get cost-sharing reduced by 75% or 50%, and cost-sharing above 5% of family income would be refundable as a tax credit.

Families would owe no MediKids premium if they show equivalent coverage (including Medicaid, SCHIP, or Medicare), and very low-income families are exempt entirely, with premiums capped at 5% of adjusted gross income for everyone else.
The bill's findings state that more than 9 million American children were uninsured at the time, and that uninsured children receive less medical and preventive care with poorer health as a result.

analysis.who_pays: Families with enrolled children would pay annual premiums through their tax filings, covering roughly a quarter of the program's per-capita cost, with exemptions and caps protecting low incomes. The Treasury's general fund would cover startup costs before premiums arrived, and the Treasury Secretary would be required to propose a schedule of progressive tax increases to fund the program as enrollment grows.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, via premiums and general federal funds

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only children born after 2006, so coverage phases in over more than two decades; a child already born in 2005 would never qualify, and full universality arrives only gradually as the age limit rises from 6 to 23.

The premium covers only about 25% of the estimated per-capita cost, and the long-term financing is deferred: the bill merely requires the Treasury Secretary to propose a schedule of progressive tax changes within a year of enactment, leaving the actual funding to a future Congress.

Families with children would owe a new tax-filing premium even if they consider their private coverage adequate, unless they affirmatively demonstrate equivalent coverage to the Secretary to have the premium waived.
A government plan paying Medicare-based rates would compete with private child coverage, which insurers and some policymakers would object to as crowding out the private market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and certain in direction: automatic, gap-free coverage for every child in a birth cohort, with the heaviest protection for low-income families. The main honest costs are financial design questions: premiums raise only about a quarter of per-capita cost, transitional money comes from the general Treasury, and the progressive taxes needed to close the gap are left unspecified for a future Congress to enact. The gradual phase-in means the bill's promise takes decades to reach everyone. The design is incremental and fiscally cautious, but its financing was deliberately left open-ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the bill on June 23, 2005 with five Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The only further action in the entire 109th Congress was a second set of introductory remarks by the sponsor on July 27, 2006; the committee held no hearing or markup and the Senate never voted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death preserved the status quo: private insurers and employers kept the children's coverage market without a competing public plan, and no new premiums or progressive taxes were imposed. Uninsured children continued to rely on Medicaid and SCHIP, with the gaps the bill aimed to close left in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers kept the children's coverage market unchanged

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor twice, in June 2005 and July 2006.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in June 2005 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 18 months of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all six sponsors were Democrats and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action.

industries.note: MediKids would be the default insurer for every child in a birth cohort, with families able to keep private coverage but always able to fall back on the public plan when other coverage lapses. A government plan paying Medicare-based rates would compete for children's coverage business that insurers otherwise hold. Its interest in defeating the bill ran against families who would have gained guaranteed coverage.

Universal child coverage would extend insured payment to care for millions of uninsured children, with provider participation and payment terms tied to Medicare. Providers and patients both gain when previously uninsured children can see a doctor.
